results.question: By how much, and how shortly before the accident, did Union Pacific change the warning-time thumbwheel setting at the Fox River Grove grade crossing?
results.expected_answer: The warning-time thumbwheel setting was reduced from 30 seconds to 25 seconds, a change made on October 11, 1995 -- about two weeks before the October 25, 1995 accident.

retrieved_chunks.text:
On October 11, 1995 -- two weeks before
the accident -- Union Pacific Railroad reset the thumbwheel to 25 seconds "to ensure consistency
at that crossing and throughout the railroad's property." UP officials stated the change did not
alter the minimum constant warning time of 20 seconds. A UP representative testified at the
Safety Board's public hearing in January 1996: "We design our circuits for 25 seconds to give a
5-second buffer... because there are conditions out on the track that make us unable to give an
exact warning time... So we put in a 5-second buffer to this 20 seconds."

DOCUMENTATION AND COMMUNICATION BETWEEN IDOT AND THE RAILROAD
On August 4, 1987, the C&NW railroad sent IDOT design plans indicating the railroad grade
crossing approach circuit lengths were "3,080 feet, 30 seconds at 70 mph." At that time no
highway traffic signals existed at Algonquin Road. In April 1991, C&NW submitted construction
prints to IDOT indicating an approach warning time for track #1 (southern track) of 25 seconds
and 30 seconds for track #2 (northern track). On May 11, 1992, C&NW provided IDOT with a
"project completion report" that answered "yes" to the question "Do all approach start distances
provide a minimum operation of 20 seconds before arrival of any train?"

At the Safety Board's public hearing in January 1996, UP presented construction prints dated July
14, 1995, indicating a minimum of 20 seconds warning time. IDOT representatives testified they
had never seen these construction prints before the hearing, and that they believed based on other
documents they had a warning time of 25 to 30 seconds from the railroad signal system. When
asked how much information about warning time the railroad provided when a signal is turned
on, the IDOT engineering technician responded: "You don't get any written documents... if we
inquired, they [the railroad] could give us an answer... We would establish some timing and put
in some test calls and we could observe how long it was from the time we received the call from
the railroad until their gates were horizontal and adjust our timing on that basis."

RAW SOURCE EXCERPT (verbatim, public domain U.S. government work)
NTSB/HAR-96/02 - Collision of METRA Train and School Bus, Fox River Grove, Illinois,
October 25, 1995
Source: https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/AccidentReports/Reports/HAR9602.pdf
Accessed: 2026-09-19
This file supplements ntsb_har9602_fox_river_grove.txt with additional verbatim detail on the
signal timing analysis, documentation history, and school busdriver background.

SCHOOL BUSDRIVER BACKGROUND (verbatim detail)
The 54-year-old school busdriver had been hired by the TJA School District on August 1, 1983,
as a secretary and bookkeeper. Between April 1986 and July 1989, she served as a bus dispatcher.
She passed the Illinois written school busdriver examination on January 2, 1987, and took the
school bus road test three times between January 2 and 5, 1987, before passing it. She was
selected on July 15, 1989, for the position of assistant transportation director, responsible for
auditing and evaluating the performance of 92 school busdrivers, though she was not herself
certified as a trainer. On the day of the accident, the regular busdriver for this route was ill, and
the substitute (the accident driver) had never driven this particular route before, either in a car or
a school bus. She had completed all but one stop on the route as the bus approached the grade
crossing.

RAILROAD SIGNAL WARNING TIME -- THUMBWHEEL HISTORY (verbatim technical detail)
The desired advance warning time for the crossing signal is entered via a "thumbwheel" switch on
the microprocessor. During the 5 years before the accident, the thumbwheel had been set at 30
seconds for the northernmost railroad track, with the narrow band shunt connected to the rails
approximately 3,053 feet from the edge of the crossing. On October 11, 1995 -- two weeks before
the accident -- Union Pacific Railroad reset the thumbwheel to 25 seconds "to ensure consistency
at that crossing and throughout the railroad's property."

The system activates the
crossing warning devices at a predetermined constant warning time regardless of the train's
speed. During the 5 years before the accident, the thumbwheel on the microprocessor at the
accident site had been set at 30 seconds for the northernmost railroad track. However, 2 weeks
before the accident (October 11, 1995), the thumbwheel was reset at 25 seconds. According to
the UP, the thumbwheel setting was changed to 25 seconds to ensure consistency at that crossing
and throughout the railroad's property.

FRA regulations address required minimum warning time in Title 49 CFR, Part 234.225,
"Activation of Warning System," which states: "A highway/rail grade crossing warning system
shall be maintained to activate in accordance with the design of the warning system, but in no
event shall it provide less than 20 seconds warning time before the grade crossing is occupied by
rail traffic."

Highway Signal System
At the accident crossing, once the microprocessor activates the crossing warning devices, the
highway signal system is simultaneously sent a signal via a "highway interconnect circuit."
Testimony from IDOT's contractors indicated that the preemption sequence could take as long as
21 seconds to reach a green indication for Algonquin Road under certain circumstances.

History of Algonquin Road
Before 1989, US 14 was a two-lane, two-way roadway. In 1989, IDOT widened US 14 using
about 35 feet of railroad property, thereby shortening the queuing area between the tracks and
US 14 from about 80 feet to about 45 feet. During the road-widening planning stages, the
railroad expressed safety concerns to IDOT and local communities about US 14 being less than
50 feet from its railroad tracks. However, IDOT completed the road-widening as planned.

Algonquin Road Grade Crossing Accident History
Safety Board investigators gathered accident information indicating that during February 1990
through September 1995, 20 accidents/incidents occurred at this crossing, resulting in no
fatalities or injuries. Nineteen accidents/incidents involved vehicles striking or being struck by
railroad gates; eleven involved commercial vehicles.

results.question: After the fatal fall at Spring Garden Station, how much did SEPTA commit to its SCOPE program, and how many outreach workers did it add?
results.expected_answer: SEPTA announced it would spend $3.6 million on the SCOPE (Safety, Cleaning, Ownership, Partnership, and Engagement) program, increasing outreach workers from 7 to 57.

retrieved_chunks.text:
AUTOPSY
Cause of death: blunt impact trauma. Manner of death: accident.

POSTACCIDENT ACTIONS
In September 2021, SEPTA announced it would spend $3.6 million on its "Safety, Cleaning,
Ownership, Partnership, and Engagement" (SCOPE) Program, increasing outreach workers from
7 to 57 to assist vulnerable populations (homelessness, addiction, mental illness) on the transit
system, creating a virtual patrol center to monitor 28,000 cameras, and equipping cleaning staff
with cell phones to streamline reporting unsafe conduct to police.

PROBABLE CAUSE
The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of the fatality was
the failure of the man on the station platform to maintain balance at the platform's edge, which
caused him to fall from the platform into the path of the train, where he was struck mid-fall by the
train and killed. Contributing to the cause of the accident was his impairment from a combination
of psychoactive drugs.

NTSB Railroad Investigation Report RIR-22/03
Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority Fatality at Spring Garden Station
Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, July 28, 2021. Issued: February 25, 2022.
Source: https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/AccidentReports/Reports/RIR2203.pdf
Accessed: 2026-09-19

THE ACCIDENT
On Wednesday, July 28, 2021, about 2:28 p.m. local time, a man was struck and killed by a train
at the Spring Garden Station platform in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. As the Southeastern
Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (SEPTA) Market-Frankford Line (MFL) passenger train
number 78 entered the station for a normal station stop, the man fell from the platform into the
path of the eastbound train and was struck and killed. Weather was mostly cloudy skies. SEPTA
is a regional public transportation authority operating bus, rapid transit, commuter rail, light rail,
and electric trolleybus services in and around Philadelphia. The Market-Frankford Line (MFL) is
a rapid transit line running from Upper Darby, Pennsylvania to the Frankford Transportation
Center (28 stations total). The Federal Transit Administration (FTA) and the Pennsylvania
Department of Transportation State Safety Oversight have federal and state oversight
responsibility for SEPTA's MFL.

NTSB investigators reviewed onboard image recorders and station surveillance video. The
deceased had been standing on the platform for several minutes while trains boarded/offloaded
passengers, then began walking toward the platform edge exhibiting an unsteady gait. MFL train
78 entered the station simultaneously for a scheduled stop; the operator was using normal braking
and was looking forward and toward the man as he approached the platform edge. At the edge,
the man took an additional step that landed his foot halfway off the edge, causing him to lose his
balance and fall into the path of the train. The train struck him as he fell.

BEFORE THE ACCIDENT
The train operator arrived on duty about 12:04 p.m. at the 69th Street Transportation Center in
Upper Darby. Review of onboard image recorders showed the operator was attentive and
operating normally throughout.

at the 69th Street Transportation Center in
Upper Darby. Review of onboard image recorders showed the operator was attentive and
operating normally throughout.

The deceased had entered the MFL at Allegheny Station and ridden a train to Spring Garden
Station (six station stops away), where he spent about 8 minutes on the platform, about 5 of them
interacting closely with another person on a bench, during which he removed his right arm from
his sweatshirt while leaving his head and left arm in it. He then began to lean and rock back and
forth, walked away from the bench toward the platform, and appeared to lose muscular dexterity
and develop an unsteady gait.

POSTACCIDENT TESTING
Investigators found the platform area had tangent track, no physical obstructions, adequate sight
distance for approaching trains, dry/regular/even walking surfaces free of debris, and a properly
installed yellow tactile warning strip. Braking performance tests on the train met or exceeded
minimum criteria.

TRAIN OPERATOR
The 52-year-old operator was a qualified SEPTA Subway-Elevated Train Operator with 7 years
of MFL experience, recertified July 11, 2019, with no issues in his most recent performance
evaluation.

TOXICOLOGY
The train operator's postaccident toxicology testing (per 49 CFR Part 655, FTA regulations) was
negative for all tested substances, as was his preemployment testing. The City of Philadelphia's
Office of the Medical Examiner independently tested the deceased man's brain tissue (no
blood/serum was available) and identified: fluoxetine (prescription antidepressant, Prozac),
methamphetamine (a stimulant, without its usual metabolite amphetamine present), fentanyl (a
potent opioid) and its metabolite despropionylfentanyl, diazepam (Valium) and its metabolites
nordiazepam and oxazepam, xylazine (a veterinary tranquilizer and human drug of abuse), and a
hydroxyzine metabolite (desalkylhydroxyzine) without the parent sedating-antihistamine drug
itself.

AUTOPSY
Cause of death: blunt impact trauma. Manner of death: accident.

results.question: How has the property-damage dollar threshold for a reportable non-rail transit collision changed between the FTA's 1997 SAMIS reporting guidance and its 2026 Safety & Security Policy Manual?
results.expected_answer: The threshold rose from a flat $1,000 in the 1997 SAMIS reporting glossary to $25,000 in the 2026 FTA Safety & Security Policy Manual for non-rail modes; rail modes instead use a "substantial damage" operational-disruption test rather than a dollar figure.

retrieved_chunks.text:
non-rail reportability thresholds. The
older 1997 SAMIS report used a narrower, threshold-based definition: "An incident in which a
transit vehicle strikes or is struck by another vehicle... Reports are made if the accident results in
death, injury, or property damage over $1,000" -- a flat $1,000 threshold, contrasted with the 2026
manual's $25,000 non-rail property-damage threshold (adjusted upward over nearly 30 years,
partly reflecting inflation and partly a policy decision to focus federal reporting on more serious
events). Researchers comparing incident counts across eras (e.g., 1997 SAMIS vs. 2021 NTST or
the 2026 manual) should account for this definitional and threshold drift rather than assuming
directly comparable "collision" counts.

CROSS-DOCUMENT NOTE -- FATALITY DEFINITION CONSISTENCY
All FTA/NTD documents in this corpus consistently define a reportable fatality as a death
confirmed within 30 days of the transit-related event, explicitly excluding deaths from illness,
natural causes, or drug overdose unrelated to the event itself. This definition has remained stable
from the 1997 SAMIS glossary through the 2026 Policy Manual, unlike the property-damage
threshold, which has changed substantially.

CROSS-DOCUMENT NOTE -- OVERSIGHT AGENCY ACRONYMS
FTA = Federal Transit Administration (federal). SSOA = State Safety Oversight Agency (state-level,
required under 49 CFR Part 659 for each state with a non-FRA-regulated rail fixed-guideway
system). TOC = Tri-State Oversight Committee (WMATA's specific SSOA, covering Virginia,
Maryland, and D.C. jointly -- the only multi-jurisdictional SSOA structured this way in the
country as of the mid-2010s). FRA = Federal Railroad Administration (regulates commuter rail
and other "commuter authority" systems under 45 USC 1104, with much stronger inspection and
enforcement powers than the FTA/SSOA framework governing rapid transit).

Safety Management Information Statistics (SAMIS) 1997 Annual Report
FTA-MA-26-5002-99-01, DOT-VNTSC-FTA-99-3
U.S. Department of Transportation, Federal Transit Administration, March 1999
Source: https://www.transit.dot.gov/sites/fta.dot.gov/files/docs/samis97.pdf
Accessed: 2026-09-19

ABSTRACT
The Safety Management Information Statistics (SAMIS) 1997 Annual Report is a compilation
and analysis of transit accident, casualty, and crime statistics reported under the Federal Transit
Administration's National Transit Database Reporting System by FTA-funded transit systems in
the United States during 1997. In its eighth year of publication, SAMIS provides uniformly
collected comprehensive safety and security data from all recipients or beneficiaries of Urbanized
Area Formula funds.

REPORTING SCOPE
Transit safety data are collected in four basic categories: Collisions, Derailments/Buses going off
road, Personal Casualties, and Fires. All transit agencies subject to NTD reporting must report
safety data. Transit security data are modeled after the FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting System,
using standardized offense definitions (Part I crime index offenses and Part II arrests). Transit
agencies serving urbanized areas (UZAs) with populations of 200,000 or more are required to
report security data. SAMIS reports property damage when it exceeds $1,000 (a lower threshold
than many other transportation industries use).

GLOSSARY OF KEY TERMS (SAFETY)
Vehicle Accident: An incident involving a moving vehicle, including collisions with another
vehicle, object, or person (except suicides) and derailment/leaving the roadway.
Collision with Vehicle/Object/People: An incident in which a transit vehicle strikes or is struck
by another vehicle, an obstacle (e.g., building, utility pole), or a person; reported if it results in
death, injury, or property damage over $1,000. Collisions with people exclude suicide attempts
unless specifically indicated.
Derailment/Left Roadway: A non-collision incident in which a transit vehicle leaves the rails or
road on which it travels (includes rollovers). All occurrences are reported, with no dollar
threshold.

Q: Is "Municipal Transit Incidents" limited to trains, or does it include buses?
A: Based on the documents in this corpus, the domain spans both. The FTA's NTD reporting
system and its SAMIS/NTST statistical publications track Motor Bus (MB) alongside all rail
modes as co-equal categories under the same Safety & Security reporting framework. Several
individual incident reports in this corpus involve buses specifically rather than rail (the NYC
MTA transit bus pedestrian fatality, HAB-18/10; the two school bus/grade-crossing collision
reports, Fox River Grove and Conasauga, though those involve school buses rather than public
transit buses specifically). The FTA-sponsored "Transit Bus Accident Investigations" background
research document treats bus-mode safety management as a full peer topic to rail-mode safety
management, using the same Safety Management System (SMS) framework required under 49
CFR Part 673 for all modes.

Q: What counts as a "reportable" event versus something transit agencies track internally but
don't have to report to the federal government?
A: This threshold has shifted over time and varies by mode, as detailed in fta_ntd_safety_
security_policy_manual_2026.txt and the cross-document reconciliation note in
fta_ntd_glossary_and_definitions_supplement.txt. As of the 2026 manual, non-rail modes report
property damage of $25,000 or more; rail modes instead use a "substantial damage" test tied to
operational disruption rather than a dollar figure. The 1997 SAMIS glossary used a flat $1,000
property-damage threshold for ALL modes -- meaning a comparison of "how many incidents
happened in 1997 vs. 2026" cannot be made by simply comparing raw incident counts, because
the definition of what qualifies as a reportable incident has moved substantially over that period.

Q: What does "R-10-3" refer to, and why does it show up in multiple unrelated reports?
A: R-10-3 is an NTSB safety recommendation number issued to the U.S.

results.question: In the WMATA Metrorail smoke and arcing incident that occurred at L'Enfant Plaza station, how many passengers were on the train and how many people were treated or transported for smoke exposure?
results.expected_answer: About 400 passengers were on the six-car train; DC Fire and EMS reported 86 people treated and transported from the scene, plus 9 more who self-transported to medical facilities (95 total), and there was 1 fatality (Carol Glover). NOTE: this is an adversarial question -- Fort Totten (9 fatalities, 2009) and Shady Grove (1 fatality, 1996) are separate WMATA incidents in this corpus that share dense Metrorail/Operations-Control-Center vocabulary with this one, so a chunker may retrieve the wrong incident's passenger or casualty figures with high similarity score.

retrieved_chunks.text:
NTSB Safety Recommendation Letter R-15-31 and R-15-32 (Urgent)
Date: September 30, 2015. To: The Honorable Anthony Foxx, Secretary of Transportation, US DOT.
Subject: WMATA Metrorail smoke and arcing accident, L'Enfant Plaza station, January 12, 2015,
and inadequate safety oversight by the Tri-State Oversight Committee (TOC).
Source: https://www.ntsb.gov/safety/safety-recs/recletters/R-15-031-032.pdf
Accessed: 2026-09-19

BACKGROUND -- THE L'ENFANT PLAZA ACCIDENT
On Monday, January 12, 2015, about 3:15 p.m. eastern standard time, WMATA Metrorail Yellow
Line train 302 stopped after encountering an accumulation of heavy smoke while traveling
southbound in a tunnel between the L'Enfant Plaza station and the Potomac River bridge in the
District of Columbia. About 400 passengers were on board the six-car train. The smoke
originated from an arcing event near the third rail about 2,000 feet south of the L'Enfant Plaza
station. Smoke filled the L'Enfant Plaza station, causing an evacuation. District of Columbia Fire
and Emergency Management Services reported that 86 people were treated and transported from
the scene; another 9 passengers self-transported to medical facilities. There was one passenger
fatality (Carol Glover, 61, died of acute respiratory failure).

Passengers spent more than 30 minutes inside the smoke-filled train before firefighters arrived. A
smoke detector near the location of heavy smoke activated at 3:04 p.m. but was not displayed at
the Rail Operations Control Center (ROCC) because of a loose wire preventing communication
with the Advanced Information Management System. WMATA's standard operating procedure
stated that at the first report of smoke, all trains should be stopped in both directions, but this did
not happen on the day of the accident.

NTSB WMATA Safety Recommendation History and Status - Cross-Reference Compilation
Compiled from references within NTSB accident reports and safety recommendation letters in
this corpus (Fox River Grove HAR-96/02, Shady Grove RAR-96/04, Fort Totten RAR-10/02,
L'Enfant Plaza oversight letter R-15-31/32).
Source: Cross-referenced from NTSB.gov accident report citations (see individual report files in
this corpus for original URLs).
Accessed: 2026-09-19
This file consolidates the recurring pattern of NTSB findings against WMATA across multiple
decades, as documented within the primary source reports already in this corpus, to aid questions
that require synthesizing information found only by reading multiple individual reports together.

TIMELINE OF MAJOR NTSB WMATA RAIL INVESTIGATIONS REFERENCED IN THIS CORPUS
1970: NTSB special study (NTSB/RSS-70/1) of WMATA's proposed safety procedures, issued
while the Metrorail system was still under construction -- resulted in one recommendation that
WMATA develop internal system safety engineering capability.
1996 (January 6): Shady Grove collision (RAR-96/04) -- train T-111 struck a standing "gap"
train after WMATA had recently eliminated routine manual train operation during winter
weather, following an internally disputed engineering conclusion about wheel flats. One fatality
(the train operator).
2009 (June 22): Fort Totten collision (RAR-10/02) -- a track circuit failure caused loss of train
detection, leading one train to strike a stopped train ahead of it. Nine fatalities, the worst accident
in Metrorail history at the time.
2015 (January 12): L'Enfant Plaza smoke/arcing incident -- an electrical short circuit near the
third rail filled a tunnel and station with smoke; one passenger fatality (Carol Glover), 86-95
people treated for smoke exposure.
2015 (August 6): Smithsonian-area derailment of nonrevenue train 412 -- caused by a "wide
gage" track defect that had been identified 27 days earlier but left in service, cited by the NTSB
as a direct illustration of the TOC's lack of enforcement authority compared to FRA-style
oversight.

Train 112, operating in
automatic mode, was traveling behind train 214. According to recorded train control system
data, the speed commands transmitted to train 112 dropped from 55 mph to 0 mph at 4:56:41,
then resumed at 55 mph about 39 seconds later, at 4:57:20. Third-rail power was lost at 4:58:08
(the moment of collision). The point of collision was on track B2 about 2,935 feet north of the
Fort Totten station.

INJURIES AND DAMAGE
Eight passengers in the lead car of train 112 and the operator of train 112 were killed (nine total
fatalities). According to the fire department, 52 patients were transported to hospitals: 2 with
critical injuries, 12 with moderate injuries, and the rest with minor injuries. Damage to train
equipment was estimated at $12 million; about $5,000 in track and appurtenance damage also
occurred.

TRAIN AND MECHANICAL INFORMATION
All six cars of train 112 were 1000-series cars manufactured by Rohr; these were the oldest cars
in the Metrorail fleet. WMATA was in the process of purchasing new 7000-series cars
(tentatively scheduled starting in 2013) to replace the 1000-series cars. After the accident,
WMATA began "bellying" the 1000-series cars (placing them in the middle of trains) to reduce
their vulnerability to catastrophic damage, though no engineering analysis had validated this
approach before it was implemented.

AUTOMATIC TRAIN CONTROL SYSTEM
The Metrorail ATC system consists of three subsystems: Automatic Train Protection (ATP),
Automatic Train Supervision (ATS), and Automatic Train Operation (ATO). The ATP subsystem
maintains train separation by transmitting speed commands based on track occupancy detected
via track circuits. Track occupancy detection uses impedance bonds and audio-frequency
signals injected into the rails; when a train's wheelsets shunt this signal, the track relay
deenergizes, indicating "occupied."

The collision occurred within a 738-foot-long track circuit designated B2-304, located about 1/2
mile north of the Fort Totten station.

results.question: What was the specific mechanical cause of the failure that allowed the Miami International Airport automated people mover train to collide with the terminal wall in 2008, and what safety system should have prevented it but did not?
results.expected_answer: A broken crystal inside the program stop module's oscillator circuit caused the train to lose the ability to determine its position and decelerate. The overspeed/overshoot relay -- the vital backup system designed to catch exactly this kind of failure -- had been disabled a week earlier by a maintenance "jumper wire" installed by a JCI technician, so it never triggered emergency braking.

retrieved_chunks.text:
NTSB/RAR-11/01
Miami International Airport, Automated People Mover Train Collision with Passenger
Terminal Wall, Miami, Florida, November 28, 2008. Adopted: November 8, 2011.
Source: https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/AccidentReports/Reports/RAR1101.pdf
Accessed: 2026-09-19 (verified live fetch)

ABSTRACT
About 4:44 p.m. on November 28, 2008, a three-car automated people mover (APM) train
operating along a fixed guideway on E Concourse at Miami International Airport failed to stop
at the passenger platform and struck a wall at the end of the guideway. A maintenance technician
was monitoring the train from the lead car, but it was operating in fully automatic mode without
a human operator. The technician and five passengers were injured; one person on the platform
also required medical attention.

THE JUMPER WIRE
The south train had been experiencing recurring failures with its wayside antenna, dynamic
braking, and overspeed/overshoot systems for weeks before the accident. On November 21,
2008 (one week before the accident), a JCI (Johnson Controls, Inc.) maintenance technician
installed a "jumper wire" between two terminals in the train's control compartment to keep it in
service while troubleshooting continued. This jumper wire bypassed the vital (safety-critical)
overspeed/overshoot relay -- the fail-safe backup system designed to stop the train if the primary
"program stop" positioning system ever failed. One JCI technician who reviewed the schematics
realized the jumper wire disabled this safety backup and told his shift lead, who directed him to
leave it in place anyway so the train could keep running. JCI had no written procedures governing
when jumper wires could be used or requiring their removal before passenger service.

WHAT ACTUALLY FAILED
Postaccident testing found the failure was a broken crystal inside the program stop module's
oscillator circuit -- the component that counted phase changes in a wayside antenna to determine
the train's position relative to its stopping point. Without a working oscillator, the train had no
way to trigger deceleration.

The report's Appendix B lists at least
22 other states with fixed-guideway systems (mostly airport people movers and amusement-park
monorails/funiculars) similarly falling outside any state oversight agency's regulated scope.

ORGANIZATIONAL ACCIDENT FRAMEWORK
The report explicitly applies James Reason's "organizational accident" framework (also cited in
the FTA bus accident investigation background research document elsewhere in this corpus),
distinguishing "active failures" (the jumper wire installation itself) from "latent failures" (MDAD's
and Florida's absent oversight, which had been dormant for two decades before this specific
active failure triggered the accident).

PROBABLE CAUSE
The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident
was the installation by Johnson Controls, Inc. maintenance technicians of a jumper wire that
prevented the overspeed/overshoot system from activating to stop the train when the crystal
within the primary program stop module failed. Contributing factors: (1) JCI's failure to provide
specific procedures regarding disabling vital train control systems during passenger operations,
(2) ineffective safety oversight by the Miami-Dade Aviation Department, (3) lack of adequate
safety oversight by the state of Florida, and (4) lack of authority by the U.S. DOT to provide
adequate safety oversight of such systems.

RECOMMENDATIONS
New recommendations went to the U.S. DOT and all 50 states/D.C. (jointly identify all fixed
guideway systems within each jurisdiction, R-11-1/R-11-2), to all 50 states/D.C. (obtain statutory
authority to oversee ALL fixed guideway systems regardless of funding source or age, R-11-3),
to Miami-Dade County (develop a system safety program plan, R-11-4), and to Johnson Controls,
Inc. (prohibit deactivation of safety-critical systems during passenger service, R-11-5). The
report also reiterates Recommendation R-10-3 (from the Fort Totten investigation, also in this
corpus) urging the DOT to seek broader rail transit safety oversight authority.

Without a working oscillator, the train had no
way to trigger deceleration. Normally the overspeed/overshoot backup system would have caught
this failure and applied emergency brakes, but the jumper wire had disabled exactly that backup.

MAINTENANCE HISTORY AND TESTING GAPS
JCI took over APM maintenance from the original contractor (Bombardier, and predecessors
back to the original 1980 manufacturer Westinghouse) in January 2008, after Bombardier
declined a new maintenance contract over liability concerns about the trains being past their
"design life." No stopping/braking tests had been conducted on either APM train before the
accident because JCI was concerned about placing stress on the aging undercarriages. The
manufacturer recommended testing vital relays every 4 years; the overspeed/overshoot relay that
had been bypassed was tagged as last inspected on December 4, 2001 -- nearly 7 years before the
accident.

POSTACCIDENT VERIFICATION TESTING
NTSB investigators conducted five stopping tests on the (undamaged) north train on December
7, 2008, WITHOUT a jumper wire installed, and the train performed within design parameters in
every test -- including correctly triggering emergency stops when simulated door-opening and
overspeed conditions were introduced. This confirmed the overspeed/overshoot system itself was
functional and would have prevented the accident had it not been bypassed.

SAFETY OVERSIGHT GAP -- A THIRD LAYER OF FAILURE
Beyond the FTA/State Safety Oversight Agency (SSOA) framework discussed elsewhere in this
corpus for FTA-FUNDED rail transit, this report reveals a distinct gap: the Miami APM system
received NO FTA funding and was therefore not covered by 49 CFR Part 659 at all. Florida's
own oversight statute (Section 341.061) was not enacted until 1984 and was not retroactive, so in
a 1988 exchange of letters, the Miami-Dade Aviation Department (MDAD) successfully argued
it did not need to develop a system safety program plan for this specific APM (built in 1980), and
no further correspondence on the topic occurred between 1988 and the 2008 accident -- 20 years
with essentially no external safety oversight of this system.
